title: Jaap Sahib
hookLine: Guru Gobind Singh's rolling praise of the Timeless, in quick changing meters

cards: Some music makes it impossible to sit still. A drumline at a parade. A song where the beat suddenly doubles and the whole crowd jumps.
Japji is calm, like a teacher talking. The next bani in the Sikh morning is something else. It gallops.
The lines are short, the rhythm keeps changing, and when a whole room recites it together it can feel like running downhill. It was written by the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh.

teach.b: Jaap Sahib is a long hymn of praise, about two hundred short verses. It isn't in the Guru Granth Sahib.
It's in a separate collection called the Dasam Granth, the book of the tenth Guru, and it's said every morning in Nitnem and at the Amrit ceremony, when Sikhs are initiated into the Khalsa.
It praises Akal, the Timeless One, and much of it describes God by what God is not.

teach.h: NO MARK, NO SIGN, NO CASTE.
teach.b: The opening, in paraphrase: the One who has no mark or sign, no color, no caste, no lineage; whose form and shape and garb no one can describe.
Then it rolls into salutations, line after line, each beginning with a word of bowing: salutation to the Timeless, to the Merciful, to the One without form, to the One without a name.
Hundreds of names, most of them saying: beyond this, beyond that. The words keep reaching, and keep admitting they can't reach. Then there's the rhythm.
Guru Gobind Singh was a poet as well as a leader, and he wrote Jaap in many different meters, chhands, switching from one to another as the hymn goes on. Some sections are slow and stately.
Some are so quick the syllables tumble.
The language mixes Braj, Sanskrit, Punjabi and even Persian and Arabic words, as if praise needed every language he knew. You don't have to follow the meaning to feel what it's doing.
It's praise with a heartbeat, and the heartbeat keeps changing.

how: Jaap Sahib, by Guru Gobind Singh, is the second bani of the Sikh morning Nitnem and is also recited during the Amrit ceremony; many Sikhs know its quick rhythms by heart.

o: a slow chant from the Guru Granth Sahib
Guru Gobind Singh's rolling hymn of praise
a battle song for the Khalsa's soldiers

games.q: what's inside Jaap Sahib — tap the pairs.
p: the book Jaap is found in

s: Jaap Sahib is in the Guru Granth Sahib
it's in the Dasam Granth, the collection of the tenth Guru.
much of Jaap describes God by what God is not
no mark, no sign, no caste, no lineage, no form anyone can describe.
Jaap is written in a single steady meter
it changes meters again and again; that's its rolling rhythm.

games.q: you're writing praise for a God beyond every description. how does Jaap Sahib do it?
o: keep saying what God is beyond, and bow again and again.
compare God to a great king.
games.why: Jaap names what God is not, no mark, no caste, no form, and salutes the Timeless line after line.

practice: If you can, play a recording of Jaap Sahib and listen for the rhythm rather than every word: where it speeds up, where it slows down, tapping the beat lightly on your knee if that helps.
If you can't play anything, sit and breathe, and notice your own rhythm, your heartbeat and your breath, praising without words.

carryVoice: Your line: the rhythm of praise. Beyond every name, and still bowing. See you in the morning.
